lesson.title: Rebuilding Europe to Save It: The Marshall Plan
lesson.summary: Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a massive American aid program to rebuild war-shattered Western Europe, aiming to remove the poverty and desperation that made communism attractive and to keep the region aligned with the United States.
lesson.body:
The Truman Doctrine had addressed an immediate crisis in Greece and Turkey, but American officials worried about a much bigger problem: the economies of Western Europe were still in ruins two years after the war ended, with damaged factories, disrupted trade, food shortages, and harsh winters making daily life miserable. Policymakers in Washington feared that desperate, hungry populations would turn to communist parties, which were already gaining strength in France and Italy, not necessarily out of ideological conviction but out of sheer economic despair.

Secretary of State George C. Marshall, a former Army general who had led American forces during World War II, proposed a solution in a commencement speech at Harvard University on June 5, 1947. Marshall called for a large scale American program to help European nations rebuild their own economies, arguing that American policy should be "directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation, and chaos." Congress passed the Economic Cooperation Act in April 1948, and over the next four years the United States sent roughly thirteen billion dollars in aid, a huge sum at the time, to participating European countries.

Marshall's offer was technically open to every European country, including the Soviet Union and its satellite states, but that was as much a political calculation as a generous one. Soviet leaders correctly suspected that accepting American aid would mean accepting American economic oversight and closer ties to the West, and Stalin ordered Soviet representatives to walk out of the planning talks in Paris and forbade Eastern European communist governments from participating. The result was that the Marshall Plan ended up reinforcing the very division of Europe it had partly been designed to prevent: Western Europe recovered quickly and remained tied to the United States, while Eastern Europe stayed poorer and more firmly under Soviet control, deepening the split between the two blocs that had begun with the Truman Doctrine.
